Newborn Care

When to Start Tummy Time and How Long Each Day

Updated: August 5, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

You can start tummy time in the first days after your baby comes home, as long as your baby is awake and you are watching the whole time. Begin with two to three short sessions a day, about three to five minutes each, and build up from there. Those few minutes strengthen the neck, shoulders, and core, and they take pressure off the back of the head. This guide covers how much to aim for, when to fit it in, and what to do when your baby objects.

Start in the first days, awake and supervised

Pediatric guidance supports starting tummy time as soon as your baby comes home from the hospital, even in the first week. Every session happens while your baby is awake, on a firm flat surface, with an adult watching the whole time. The umbilical cord stump is not a reason to wait; gentle pressure on the belly is fine, though you can pause for a few days if the area seems tender. If your baby was born early or has a medical condition, ask your care team when and how to begin, since the right start can look a little different.

The line worth memorizing is back to sleep, tummy to play. Sleep always happens on the back; tummy time only happens when your baby is awake and someone is right there. If your baby starts to drift off during a session, roll them onto their back or move them to their usual sleep space. Skip tummy time on couches, beds, and other soft surfaces, and never walk away, even for a moment. A newborn's head is heavy for their neck, and a face pressed into soft padding is the risk you are guarding against.

How long, and how many times a day

Begin with two to three sessions a day, each around three to five minutes. Over the first weeks, let sessions stretch as your baby tolerates them, aiming for roughly 15 to 30 total minutes a day. By about 3 months, many babies can handle close to an hour a day, still broken into short bursts rather than one long stretch. Treat these numbers as a direction, not a quota. Thirty seconds here and a minute there all count, and a difficult day where you manage very little does not undo the progress you have already made.

Frequent and short works better than rare and long. Watch your baby rather than the clock: lifting the head, propping on forearms, and looking around mean the session is working, while a face flat on the mat and escalating crying mean it is time to stop. Ending before a full meltdown makes the next attempt easier, because tummy time stays a neutral event instead of a fight. If it helps to see the pattern, jot session lengths in BeMama or on paper for a week; most parents are surprised how quickly a few daily minutes add up.

Why a few minutes on the tummy matter

Tummy time is strength training scaled to a newborn. Working against gravity in this position builds the neck, shoulder, arm, and core muscles your baby will use for head control, then for pushing up on forearms, and eventually for rolling and sitting. Those later skills have their own timelines, but they all draw on the same foundation, and awake time on the tummy is where that foundation gets built. It also gives your baby practice turning the head to both sides and shifting weight from side to side, small movements that matter more than they look.

There is a second reason. Babies sleep on their backs for safety, which means the back of the head spends many hours against a firm mattress. Regular awake time on the tummy takes pressure off that spot and helps reduce the flat areas that can develop on a young skull. Alternating which end of the crib your baby's head points toward, and which arm you hold them in for feeds, helps too. Mild flattening is common and often improves with position changes, but it is worth mentioning at a checkup if you notice it.

The best time of day, and what to lay out

Timing decides how a session goes. The friendliest windows are after a diaper change or shortly after a nap, when your baby is rested, alert, and not hungry. Right after a full feed is the hardest slot: pressure on a full stomach invites spit-up and fussing, so wait roughly 20 to 30 minutes after eating when you can. Skip attempts when your baby is overtired or clearly hungry, because a session that starts in tears teaches your baby that the floor is a bad place to be. Two calm minutes beat ten miserable ones.

The setup is simple. Spread a clean blanket or firm play mat on the floor, away from pets and foot traffic, and lay your baby down on their front. Then get down there too. Your face, eight to twelve inches away, is the most interesting object in the room, so talk, sing, and pull faces. A high-contrast card, a board book propped open, or an unbreakable baby mirror placed just within view gives their eyes something to work toward. Rotate what they see between sessions so the position stays new instead of stale.

When your baby protests, and when to ask for help

Plenty of healthy newborns complain the moment they land on their front, and that protest is not a verdict on you or them. Several positions count as tummy time without the flat floor: lie back at a recline with your baby on your chest, place them tummy down across your lap while you sit, or carry them face down along your forearm with their head and neck supported near your elbow and your hand under the chest. A small rolled towel under the chest and armpits, arms forward, can also make the floor version less frustrating. Seconds count, and frequency matters more than duration.

A few patterns deserve a clinician's eyes. Mention it at a well visit, or call sooner, if your baby always turns the head to the same side, strongly resists turning one way, is developing a noticeable flat spot, feels unusually stiff or floppy, or shows little gain in head control over several weeks of regular practice. These things are often easy to address when caught early, sometimes with simple position changes or exercises a pediatrician or physical therapist can show you. Your baby's own clinician knows their history and is the best judge of what is typical for them.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Early development includes social attention, sounds, movement, feeding, and growing head control. Milestone lists describe skills most children can do by an age; they are observation prompts, not standardized developmental screening tests.

Supervised awake tummy time can be built gradually in short sessions. A baby should still be placed on their back for sleep, and loss of a skill or caregiver concern should be discussed rather than waiting for the next checklist age.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama to save dated observations, activities, growth entries, and questions. The app does not score development or diagnose delay.

When to seek help

Contact the baby’s healthcare professional for concerns about movement, hearing, vision, feeding, interaction, or loss of a skill; seek urgent care for an acute change or seizure-like activity.

Links lead directly to guidance from the organizations named above.

Key takeaways

  • Start tummy time in the first days home, always awake and always supervised.
  • Begin with two to three sessions of about three to five minutes a day.
  • Work toward 15 to 30 total minutes daily, and about an hour in short bursts by 3 months.
  • Try it after a nap or diaper change, and wait a short while after feeds.
  • Chest to chest and across the lap positions count when the floor is a battle.

Frequently asked questions

How long should tummy time be for a newborn?

About three to five minutes per session is plenty for a newborn, two to three times a day. Over the early weeks, build toward roughly 15 to 30 total minutes daily as your baby tolerates more. Short, frequent sessions work better than one long stretch, and even 30 seconds counts.

Should you do tummy time after feeding?

It is better to wait roughly 20 to 30 minutes after a feed before starting tummy time. Pressure on a full stomach makes spit-up and fussing more likely. A window after a diaper change or a nap, when your baby is rested and not hungry, usually goes best.

What if my baby hates tummy time?

Keep sessions very short and switch to positions your baby tolerates, like lying tummy down on your chest while you recline or across your lap while you sit. Both still build the same muscles. Try again after a nap, get face to face on the floor, and end before a full meltdown. Most babies protest less as their strength grows.

Why is tummy time important?

Tummy time builds the neck, shoulder, arm, and core strength a baby needs for head control and, later, skills like rolling and sitting. It also takes pressure off the back of the head, which helps reduce flat spots, since babies sleep on their backs for safety. A few supervised minutes several times a day is enough to get those benefits.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
